title: Continental Breakup–driven Uplift Instigated East Antarctic Ice Sheet Formation | Science
abstract: Why Antarctica became glaciated ∼34 million years ago (Ma) remains debated, as relatively warm climates and sea temperatures appear inconsistent with ice sheet formation. Although a critical decline in CO2 is considered primarily responsible, evidence ...

method: The study uses geological and geophysical data to model the uplift caused by continental breakup and its effect on climate and ice sheet initiation.
result: Continental breakup-driven uplift created highlands that allowed ice sheet formation even under relatively warm conditions, challenging the view that CO2 decline alone was responsible.
conclusion: Tectonic processes, specifically continental breakup, can instigate ice sheet formation by creating high-elevation regions, highlighting the interplay between geology and climate.

title: Institutionalizing Ai Diplomacy In Africa | Science
abstract: The contemporary landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) diplomacy in Africa is structurally bound to the continent’s history of science, technology, and innovation (STI) engagement. Since the nineteenth century, the African continent has been positioned primarily as a target of external scientific inquiry rather than an active participant in global knowledge production. Colonial-era scientific expeditions sought to catalog geological resources and ecological assets to feed the industrial economies of Western countries, establishing a systemic dependency that relegated Africa to the periphery of the global natural resource trade and other strategic mineral markets. This legacy shaped an international order in which technological advancements across North America, Europe, and East Asia frequently occur through the extraction of African resources, without corresponding technology transfer or local capacity building.
tldr: The paper discusses the historical and structural challenges of AI diplomacy in Africa, focusing on colonial legacies and resource extraction.
motivation: To analyze how Africa's historical position as a resource provider rather than knowledge producer affects its current AI diplomacy efforts.
method: Historical analysis and policy discussion based on the legacy of colonial science and technology engagement.
result: Identifies systemic dependencies and lack of technology transfer that hinder Africa's participation in global AI governance.
conclusion: Calls for institutionalizing AI diplomacy in Africa to overcome historical imbalances and foster local capacity building.

title: Family Stability Sustains Scientific Talent | Science
abstract: Recent US immigration actions show how quickly legal pathways to permanent residence can become uncertain. US Citizenship and Immigration Services has also announced that adjustment of status will be granted only in extraordinary circumstances, signaling that many temporary residents seeking green cards may need to apply through consular processing abroad (2, 3). These policies do not only affect scientists, yet they raise a science-policy concern: Family instability can weaken the retention of foreign-born researchers.
tldr: This paper discusses how US immigration policies affecting family stability can hinder the retention of foreign-born scientists.
motivation: Recent US immigration actions have created uncertainty for foreign researchers, potentially weakening the scientific workforce.

title: Stop The Biodiversity Sampling Arms Race | Science
abstract: Global biodiversity is in crisis, with wild vertebrate populations declining by 69% since 1970 (1). At the same time, advances in high-throughput genetic sequencing and an increase in international collaborations have shifted biodiversity research toward data-intensive paradigms, in which single studies may now involve thousands of specimens and large quantities of species-level data (2). But must biodiversity breakthroughs depend on substantial biological sampling? In our opinion, the answer is no. Instead, we believe that study sample size should be determined on the basis of scientific justifications.
tldr: This paper argues that biodiversity research should not rely on massive sampling but on scientifically justified sample sizes.
motivation: Global biodiversity is declining rapidly, and current data-intensive approaches often prioritize large sample sizes over scientific rigor.
method: The authors present an opinion piece critiquing the 'sampling arms race' and advocating for study design based on statistical power and research questions.
result: No empirical results; the paper is a perspective calling for a shift in research culture.
conclusion: Biodiversity studies should determine sample sizes based on scientific justification rather than competing for the largest dataset.
